records.name: Sri Lanka
records.summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Sections 365/365A of the Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women); prosecutions limited but harassment, violence, extortion, arbitrary arrests and denial of services are frequent; no comprehensive anti-discrimination protections; authorities use forced anal and vaginal examinations to seek evidence - widely condemned as torture. Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Sri Lanka's criminalisation of same-sex activity.

ICJ opinion piece (Aug 2023) by Mathuri Thamilmaran: 'Protecting transgender persons: Going beyond rule by circular' - the Sri Lanka Police are the foremost perpetrators of human-rights violations against LGBTI individuals; recent months saw both the Police and the Human Rights Commission acknowledging this; argues administrative circulars are insufficient without legal reform.

UK Home Office CPIN Sri Lanka: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (v6.0, Sept 2024): assessment of risk from state and non-state actors, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with detailed country information.

US State Department country report for Sri Lanka (custom URL): official human-rights assessment including the SOGI section - criminalisation under the penal code and police harassment of LGBT persons.

Joint UPR stakeholder report (EQUAL GROUND, Northwestern CIHR, GIHR) for Sri Lanka's 3rd cycle: 'Human Rights Violations Against LGBTIQ Individuals in Sri Lanka' - documents criminalisation and violations by the coalition of NGOs for UPR.

Canada IRB Response to Information Request LKA103948.E (Jan 2012): 'Treatment of sexual minorities in Sri Lanka' - Article 365 criminalises 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' (up to 10 years, men only); Article 365A 'gross indecency' (both sexes, amended 1995 to cover women); rarely enforced with no convictions, but criminalisation 'paves the way for police and anti-gay groups to brand all lesbian, bisexual, transgendered persons as perverts and criminals'.

records.name: Mongolia
records.summary:
Mongolia is a country workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and identity grounds were added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; police guidance requires officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identification documents, a favourable enforcement practice.

The realistic risk for a visitor is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside the capital's central districts, where social acceptance is low.

sources.summary: Outright International (last updated 12 March 2026): consensual same-sex intimacy decriminalised 1993; sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination prohibited but protections fragmented (no comprehensive law); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited with no union recognition; groups can register.
thin: no usable finding

The Establishment (Aug 2018): profiles Anaraa Nyamdorj, trans man and co-founder/advisor of the LGBT Centre — came out in 2004, began transition in 2011; describes Mongolia's 2018 Pride and LGBT Centre advocacy; ground on trans life, transition access and acceptance in Ulaanbaatar.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2019): after an officer assaulted a detained transgender woman, the LGBT Center trained police on the 2017 criminal code's hate-crime provisions — 500+ police officers, prosecutors and judges trained; force now has guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of ID documents.

GlobalGayz Mongolia report: no laws specifically against homosexuality though 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' provisions remain; the scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism; a 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties where attendees fear being outed.

records.name: Ecuador
records.summary:
Ecuador is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016, and the legal framework is now among the region's strongest. The 2024 reform lets adults change name and sex/gender on the identity document directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery), and in 2024-25 court rulings extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: a monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and the "internal armed conflict" against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024, with two more LGBTQ people killed in its first weeks; Quito and Guayaquil, the two main cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.

sources.summary: Primicias (12 Jun 2024): President Noboa issued on 11 Jun 2024 the reglamento to the National Assembly's 12 Dec 2023 reforms of the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, streamlining civil-registry gender-marker changes — the operative procedure for legal gender recognition.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Los Angeles Blade piece (Jan 2024) reports violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians increasing amid the internal armed conflict.
AP (Apr 2026): 'A transgender teen's case in Ecuador opens path for others seeking legal recognition' — Constitutional Court rulings let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Ecuador: documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption - baseline context.

2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences and sexual orientation and identity — the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

PinkNews (31 May 2018): the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon (child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon); lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said refusal violated the child's rights — a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

records.name: Jamaica
records.summary:
Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life.

Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

sources.summary: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

Amnesty International urgent appeal (4 Jun 2006): reports vigilante violence and police ill-treatment or torture of LGBT people in Jamaica — gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once orientation known; lesbians raped and driven into asylum abroad; concern that prominent musicians promote homophobia.

records.name: Trinidad and Tobago
records.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

sources.summary: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (23 Aug 2024): the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution (decision announced at a special convention); CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'. Documents LGBTQ-rights exclusion from the 2024 constitutional-review process.

GlobalGayz (Aug 2012): travel/culture profile stating that although homosexuality is illegal 'the laws are mostly ignored' in practice; describes tourist-facing social scene and island context. Usable as a 2012 non-enforcement baseline; predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so dated for current-law purposes.

PinkNews (21 Nov 2017): first-person appeal by activist Jason Jones during his High Court challenge to T&T's same-sex criminalisation — he faces up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner; article carries the litigation campaign. Marks the constitutional challenge that put the criminal law in play.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 Jun 2016): PM Keith Rowley told Parliament (17 Jun 2016) the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws; cites Newsday. Documents the reform-refusal gap in official rhetoric as of 2016.

records.name: Ghana
records.summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

sources.summary: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Feb 2024) covers Ghana's parliament passing the anti-LGBT bill.

Human Rights Watch (5 Mar 2024): called on Ghana's president to veto the anti-LGBT bill — the page's call to 'veto the bill' is readable; bill sharply increased penalties and criminalised advocacy (bill itself later lapsed — see superseded note on the BBC/JURIST entries).

BBC: Ghana's Supreme Court unanimously dismissed two challenges to the anti-LGBT bill — Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson: 'Until there's presidential assent, there is no act', review deferred until the president signs; petitioners' lawyers said they would explore options. SUPERSEDED: Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

JURIST (Feb 2024): Parliament passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill 2021 unanimously after its third reading — up to 3 years for identifying as LGBTQ+, up to 5 years for forming or funding LGBTQ+ groups. SUPERSEDED: Ghana's 2024 anti-LGBTQ 'Human Sexuality' bill lapsed unsigned when Parliament dissolved pre-2024 election; colonial 'unnatural carnal knowledge' criminalisation persists; Pres. Mahama signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill

HRW report (Jan 2018) 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am': full PDF - violence and discrimination against LGBT people in Ghana; section 104(1)(b) criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

HRW report landing page (8 Jan 2018), 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People in Ghana' — full report and annex downloads; endnotes document 2017 victim interviews (Kumasi, Tamale) and police/vigilante violence.

Bachelor thesis (Diaconia University of Applied Sciences, Helsinki, 2017) by Seree Yeboa-Mensa: survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland on LGBT rights in Ghana - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.
